extracted.intended_audience: conference organizers, program chairs, peer-review researchers, AI ethics/policy makers, and reviewers considering or designing AI-augmented review systems
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and empirical criteria for evaluating whether and how to deploy LLMs in scholarly peer review, including necessary conditions, measurement methods, attack modes, and evaluation requirements. Focused on conference-style peer review (e.g., ICLR/ICML/NeurIPS) but applicable more broadly to academic review pipelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: C1 (review diversity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Review diversity is a necessary condition: AI reviewers must preserve the diversity of perspectives present in human peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure diversity with manual inspections and complementary metrics (see IntraSim and InterSim). High textual/semantic similarity across reviews implies reduced information gain from multiple reviewers. Restricting analysis to weaknesses and questions sections is a partial proxy for argumentative/content diversity. Even if diversity condition is met, it is necessary but not sufficient for safe automation.

rubrics_metrics.name: C2 (non-gameability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-gameability is a necessary condition: AI reviewers must not be trivially gameable by purely stylistic or zero-shot automated rewrites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrated failure mode: 'paper laundering' (zero-shot LLM rewrites of LaTeX that increase AI reviewer scores without substantive scientific improvement). A system that can be trivially gamed (e.g., score increases via cosmetic edits) should not influence acceptance decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adversarial robustness testing (Requirement 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any AI system used in peer review must demonstrate resistance to manipulation, including prompt injection and zero-shot laundering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before deployment, conduct red-team evaluations and adversarial robustness testing to systematically test manipulation strategies. Systems failing such tests must not be used to shape acceptance decisions. Tests should include prompt injection, targeted textual perturbations, and zero-shot rewrite laundering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validated accuracy with acceptable false positive rates (Requirement 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: AI tools (especially error-detection tools) must demonstrate validated accuracy and acceptable false positive rates before influencing reviewer judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Error-detection tools may be useful for authors' self-checks but current systems report unacceptably high false positive rates (e.g., up to ~35%). Use validated benchmarks and require higher precision for tools that will affect decisions. Specify acceptable error thresholds and report false positive/negative rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency about AI deployment (Requirement 3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conference organizers must publicly disclose system prompts, model versions, and integration details for any AI tools used in the review process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public release of integration details enables independent audit, helps identify biases, and builds trust. Examples: publish system prompts, model IDs, configuration choices, where in the pipeline models are used (pre-screening, feedback, review-writing, meta-review), and any automated decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Task suitability: automate only easily verifiable tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all peer review tasks are equally suited to automation: tasks with easily verifiable outputs (e.g., formatting errors, hallucinated references) may be appropriate for AI assistance; tasks relying on authentic human judgment are not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer AI assistance for verifiable checks where human validation is cheap. Avoid delegating accept/reject judgments and other non-verifiable evaluative judgments to AI without rigorous validation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical studies on stakeholder values
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions on automation boundaries must be grounded in empirical studies of stakeholder values (authors, reviewers, organizers, and the public).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct large-scale surveys and deliberative processes to elicit values (e.g., fairness, timeliness, reviewer expertise recognition) and trade-offs. Use these empirical results to set community-defined requirements and update them over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: User studies on human–AI interaction in reviewing
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand how AI assistance affects reviewer behavior via user studies, including risks of overreliance and changes in diversity of opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study whether reviewers catch AI errors or propagate them, how interfaces affect critical engagement, whether AI suggestions reduce argumentative diversity, and how to design interfaces that promote independence. Run randomized trials similar to prior large-scale deployments (e.g., ICLR/NeurIPS experiments) to measure downstream effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rethinking incentive structures for human reviewing
rubrics_metrics.description: Rather than replacing humans, improve incentives and structures so human expertise is valued and reviewer quality increases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest in reviewer incentives, recognition, and workflow improvements to reduce rushed reviews. Consider incentive reforms as part of any strategy to address review load before resorting to automation of judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement methodology: IntraSim and InterSim (diversity metrics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Operationalize review diversity with IntraSim (intra-paper inter-reviewer similarity) and InterSim (inter-paper intra-reviewer similarity) computed on review embeddings using cosine similarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IntraSim(p) = average pairwise sim between reviews of the same paper; InterSim(p,q) = average sim between reviews of different papers written by same reviewer type. Use text embeddings (authors used OpenAI text-embedding-3-small) and cosine similarity; interpret high similarity as linguistic/semantic homogenization. Control for confounds (e.g., text length) and consider restricting to weaknesses/questions sections to focus on substantive critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictive validity requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: AI review scores should have validated predictive validity (e.g., predict final acceptance decisions) comparable to human reviewers before being used to make or heavily influence decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare AUCs and correlations: the paper shows averaged human scores predict ICLR acceptance better (AUC = 0.822) than averaged AI scores (AUC = 0.710). Require comparable or superior predictive performance (with non-overlapping CIs) before allowing AI to shape outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitoring and mitigation of intellectual monoculture
rubrics_metrics.description: Monitor whether AI systems cause convergence of scientific writing styles or incentives toward homogeneous presentation ('intellectual monoculture').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure pairwise similarity between paper embeddings (e.g., abstracts+introductions) before and after AI rewriting; the paper reports laundered papers becoming significantly more similar (+6.5%). If systems incentivize homogeneity, design countermeasures (e.g., penalize style-only improvements, diversify training/data, preserve plural evaluation signals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition/precaution: no automation of acceptance-relevant judgment without rigorous evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not allow AI to automate judgment relevant to acceptance decisions without prior rigorous scientific evaluation demonstrating safety, robustness, and legitimacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the paper's central normative stance: automated judgments affecting publication outcomes should be subject to pre-deployment trials, audits, red-team tests, and community deliberation. Distinguish AI assistance (allowed with oversight) from AI replacement of human judgment (disallowed until proven safe).

rubrics_metrics.name: Require public audits and reproducible evaluation studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Before deployment, AI reviewing tools should be evaluated via reproducible studies (randomized trials, tool evaluations) whose methods and results are publicly available for scrutiny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite examples like the ICLR 2025 Review Feedback Agent study and planned NeurIPS experiments. Publish datasets, prompts, model versions, pre/post metrics, and analysis code to enable independent replication and auditing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detection and enforcement considerations (policy realism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Policies prohibiting AI use are hard to enforce due to detection difficulty; nevertheless, the recommended approach focuses on evaluating deployed systems rather than policing individual reviewer behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design policies and incentives that encourage trustworthy reviewer behavior, focus on tool-level evaluation and deployment decisions, and consider realistic detection limits. Use audits and transparency rather than relying solely on prohibition/enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsible authoring and AI-generated content accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors remain responsible for all paper contents, including AI-generated text; fully automated laundering introduces risks (plagiarism, fabricated content) and ethical/legal accountability concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discourage fully automated, unchecked rewrites used to game reviewers. Require authors to verify any AI-generated content; encourage declarations of AI use per conference policies and institutional norms.
